catalog_quote: ACCENT. The accent is almost always on the penult. EXAMPLES. I->£a-du, a hand; v^-ke, give; e-ja-nga-na-if^-bo, a book; le- va-i»-de, show. Exception 1. Verbs followed by a monosyllabic objective. EXAMPLE. Y^Jke 'mba, give me; Levaki<// ma, show him. Here the accent is carried forward to the last syllables ke and d6. But indeed this exception ie only apparent, and would disappear if the pronom- inal objectives 'mba and ma were written, as in He- brew, as suffixes to their verbs, thus; v6k6mba, le- vakidemd. Exception 2. The word beja, food, and perhaps a few others, like miba, water, and diba, marriage, seem to accentuate the last syllable.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is present verbatim in the held Mackey/Nassau 1892 scanned and on the page scan at book p.18 (p.23), with the p.44 and p.61 cross-references also confirmed. (2) The classification (weight-blind penult, clitic counted, listed final-accent exceptions) rests on a 1892 missionary/pedagogical grammar. Against Glottolog's 13 descriptive refs there is no later reference grammar; the only modern phonology is Essono 1988 (unpublished) / Essono 1990 (11-pp ASG sketch in RGSH 2), not yet obtained and not online; web search (Sorosoro, fr.wikipedia, SIL archive, Google Books) found no instrumental or tonal study of Benga itself, and Sorosoro explicitly says Benga tonology is little known. sources.quote: 'El acento, que marca su sonido peculiar, sólo se halla en las vocales á, é, ú' (accent mark = vowel quality/length, not word stress); no penult rule. Held full scanned (line ~19306) adds that homographic verbs (yaka 'dormir' vs yaka 'llorar') are distinguished 'por medio del acento ó pronunciación' -- suggestive of lexical tone, not of a different stress position.
